Saint Bernard Planning: Food, Space, Drool, and Time

A Saint Bernard is a giant, cold-loving companion with a shorter lifespan. Plan for big meals, drool, warm-weather limits, and joints with this worksheet.

Published: 2026-10-04Sources checked: 3Educational planning guide

A Saint Bernard is a calm, devoted giant that eats a lot, drools, dislikes heat, and typically lives only about eight to ten years, so planning is really about scale, comfort, and making the most of a shorter life.

Start with scale

The numbers set the tone. VCA lists the Saint Bernard at about 25 to 28 inches tall, roughly 120 to 200 pounds, with a life expectancy of about 8 to 10 years. It was the original search-and-rescue dog of the St. Bernard Hospice in the Alps, and VCA describes it today as a calm, well-mannered, loyal, and generally child-friendly housedog that can be stubborn and somewhat aloof with strangers, learning quickly but needing a firm, reward-based approach.

Everything a Saint Bernard needs is sized up: bigger food portions, a bigger bed, a vehicle that fits it, and a plan for the day its joints or age make stairs hard. The short lifespan also means health planning starts early rather than at middle age. A 150-pound dog is not simply a bigger version of a Labrador; the logistics of feeding, transporting, medicating, and caring for it in old age are a different scale of commitment, and it helps to be honest about that before you fall for the face.

Heat, comfort, and drool

VCA notes the Saint Bernard enjoys cold weather but does not do well in warm weather, and its warm-weather rating is the lowest on the scale while its cold-weather rating is the highest. In hot climates, air conditioning, shade, and cool-hour activity are part of basic care, not luxuries, and the ASPCA adds that any dog spending time outdoors needs shade and plenty of cool water in the heat.

VCA is blunt that owners should be prepared for drool. That means towels by the door, wiping the face after meals and water, and accepting some cleanup as routine. Grooming itself is modest: VCA says the coat can be smooth or long, needs only occasional brushing about once a week to remove dead hair, and that shedding is average. So the Saint's upkeep is less about the coat and more about comfort, cleanup, and space for a very large, calm housedog that VCA describes as loyal and generally good with children under supervision.

Food, growth, and joints

Feeding a giant is a real budget line. VCA notes Saints tend to stay in good weight or run slightly overweight, and that puppies should be fed a large-breed growth food, which slows the growing rate but not the final size and may reduce the incidence or severity of hip dysplasia in adults. That growth-rate detail matters: with giant breeds, feeding for fast growth can work against the joints you are trying to protect.

Joints matter for any giant. The Orthopedic Foundation for Animals explains that hip dysplasia stems from an abnormally developed hip joint and that, over time, the cartilage breaks down and can cause pain with movement. The OFA stresses that weight control and appropriate exercise are central to management, describing a lean body condition where the ribs are easily felt and there is a visible waistline. It also notes preliminary hip screening is available for dogs between 4 and 23 months, and that OFA classifies hips as Excellent, Good, Fair, Borderline, Mild, Moderate, or Severe.

Set up your home to spare the joints from day one; our joint mobility home setup guide and stairs and ramp budget help you plan floors, beds, and access before problems appear.

Feeding routine and bloat awareness

The ASPCA's general dog care guidance notes that for some dogs, including larger canines or those prone to bloat, it is better to feed two smaller meals rather than one large one. For a chest-deep giant like the Saint Bernard, a considered feeding routine is worth discussing with your veterinarian rather than defaulting to a single big bowl.

This guide does not diagnose or treat any condition, and it cannot tell you whether a particular dog is at risk. What it can do is flag that meal structure is a reasonable question to raise. Ask your veterinarian how to split meals, whether to slow fast eating, and what warning signs should prompt an urgent call. Pair that with the ASPCA's reminder to keep clean, fresh water available at all times.

A realistic week (and a short lifetime)

On a summer day you exercise early, keep the house cool, and wipe drool through the day. You buy food in bulk because a giant empties a bag fast. You back the car up to a ramp because lifting a Saint is not a one-person job. And because VCA gives a lifespan of about 8 to 10 years, you front-load vet relationships and joint care rather than waiting.

  • Daily: a moderate cool-hour walk; drool cleanup; measured meals.
  • Weekly: a brush-through; a body and joint once-over.
  • Ongoing: weight control and easy access to floors and the car.

Questions for a breeder, rescue, or vet

  • Ask a breeder whether the parents have OFA hip and elbow evaluations, and what the grades were.
  • Ask what large-breed puppy diet the dog is on and why.
  • Ask a rescue about the dog's mobility, weight history, and any joint concerns.
  • Ask a veterinarian how to monitor body condition on a giant frame.
  • Ask what a joint or emergency visit typically involves for a dog this size at your clinic.

Common mistakes with giants

  • Overfeeding a growing puppy, when VCA notes large-breed growth food is meant to slow the growth rate.
  • Exercising hard in heat, which VCA warns this cold-loving breed tolerates poorly.
  • Skipping a ramp and risking injury lifting the dog.
  • Delaying joint-friendly home changes until mobility is already declining.
  • Underestimating how much a giant's food and prevention cost each month.

What this guide cannot tell you

This guide cannot tell you a specific Saint Bernard's lifespan, whether it will develop joint disease, or your local prices. It offers no diagnosis, treatment, or dosing. The OFA notes that the appearance and timing of clinical signs vary widely between dogs. Use local quotes for the worksheet, and rely on a licensed veterinarian for health decisions and screening advice for your individual dog.

FAQ

How much does a Saint Bernard cost to feed?
There is no single figure, because portions scale with a 120-to-200-pound frame and local food prices differ. VCA notes Saints should eat a balanced diet with calories restricted if they gain weight, and giant puppies eat large-breed growth food. Estimate your own cost by multiplying a bag's price by how many bags a month your dog goes through at giant-breed portions.
Can a Saint Bernard handle hot weather?
Not well. VCA states the Saint Bernard enjoys cold weather but does not do well in warm weather, giving it the lowest warm-weather rating. In hot climates, owners rely on air conditioning, shade, plenty of water, and exercise during cooler hours. Watch closely for signs of overheating in summer, and contact a veterinarian if your dog struggles in the heat.
Why is the Saint Bernard's lifespan so short?
VCA lists a life expectancy of about 8 to 10 years, which is typical for giant breeds; larger dogs generally live fewer years than small ones. This guide cannot explain the biology in detail or predict an individual dog's lifespan. The practical takeaway is to build a veterinary relationship early and plan joint and preventive care from the start rather than waiting for old age.
